Someone answering “questions for emudhra” also say the keys were intended to be exported to US and EU data centers. I don’t know if that would have precluded inspection (hopefully it’s encrypted some way, but why not have the destination HSM generate the CSR?)Edit: I see the below paragraph is quoted extensively below. I hadn’t seen those comments yet. Oh wellSource: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449#c11Content:We have done some preliminary assessment, there appears to be a flaw in the KGC script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys, our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the csr (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo)The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted.
Some additional context - these issuers created were meant for export to our US and European data centers to solve data sovereignty issues for some of our customers (but never ended up operationally in production except for one).reply

Wrapping/unwrapping means the HSM would generate the private key and then encrypt it with a key only known to the other HSMs. Those other HSMs would then decrypt the key on import. The private key should still have been impossible to examine outside the HSMs.reply

first_paragraph: 20th October 2026The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.To demonstrate that the keys are compromised, the original reporter Wayne signed the following message with the private key of each of the eight intermediate CAs and reported it to the Root Program Teams on the 17th of October:We have a problem here - Wayneproof.zip contains the message, and for each intermediate the certificate, its public key and a signature on the message. To verify with OpenSSL:The root programs and many downstream trust stores have taken action to protect their users. The certificates have been blocked in Firefox and Chrome since the 17th of October, in Apple devices since the 19th and on Microsoft platforms since the 20th.The issue was responsibly disclosed to downstream trust stores on the 19th of October. Many have already released updates

What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI?October 19, 2026Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father.My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?Mr. Edison says
That the radio will supplant the teacher.
Already one may learn languages by means
Of Victrola records.
The moving picture will visualize
What the radio fails to get across.
Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods.
With fire-horses,
And long-haired women;
Or, perhaps shown in museums.
Education will become a matter

And if anything, Apple’s culture has been overtuned towards not providing that control, if at all possible.Nobody wants complexity for complexity’s sake, but this is the type of thing that should have come up in a meeting, and someone didn’t feel empowered to bring it up.reply

It's a while since I used Airplay for anything other than Youtube videos, but here is how I thought it worked:1. If I choose to Airplay from the control center, it mirrors the whole screen (or possibly also extends as a second screen). Whatever I open on the iPad (or drag to the second screen) is what the audience sees.2. If I Airplay from inside an app with presentation mode, it works similar to Airplaying a video. That one app remains active even if I switch to another app.3. To switch what gets presented, I simply start a new Airplay session: from control center if I want to switch to sharing the whole screen, or to another app if I want that app's presentation mode. This doesn't have to be automatic, but I shouldn't have to actively close the old session to start a new one.4. To switch back to a previous presentation, I open that app back up and re-enable Airplay - there could be a button to "resume presentation".Maybe I'm missing something, but I don't see how that is too complicated.
